marks.gloss_en: דומיא דעמיתך: מה עמיתך באחת, אף גוי נמי באחת
מיתיבי ... ואי אמרת מעות קונות, משיכה למה לי? -- if money acquires from a gentile, why does the baraita turn on pulling?
one who buys gerutaot from gentiles and finds an idol among them: if he pulled before paying, he returns it; if he pulled after paying, he takes the benefit to the Dead Sea
הכא במאי עסקינן -- שקיבל עליו לדון בדיני ישראל (= p_okimta_kibel_alav, itself attacked twice below)
אי הכי, מעות למה לי? -- if Jewish law, why mention money?
הכי קאמר: אף על פי שנתן מעות, אי משיך -- אין, ואי לא -- לא
the stam: the baraita speaks where [the gentile] accepted to be judged by Jewish law
מדרישא משיכה אינה קונה, סיפא נמי ... ואיידי דתנא רישא משך תנא סיפא נמי משך (= p_rav_ashi_meshicha_einah_konah)
Rav Ashi: from the first clause, pulling does not acquire; so in the latter too; 'pulled' is said in the latter only because the first said it
מדסיפא משיכה קונה, רישא נמי ... רישא: לא נתן ולא משך -- יחזור בדברים (= p_ravina_meshicha_konah)
Ravina: from the latter clause, pulling acquires; so in the first too; and the first means: if he neither paid nor pulled, he may retract -- retract in words
אי הכי, קשיא רישא -- in the first clause he pulled and still returns it
רישא משום דאיכא מקח טעות (= p_abaye_reisha_mekach_taut)
רישא משום דאיכא מקח טעות, סיפא ליכא מקח טעות? -- is the latter clause not a mistaken purchase too?
Abaye: the first clause [he returns it] because it is a mistaken purchase
רישא וסיפא מקח טעות; the first does not look like an idol in a Jew's hand, the latter does (= p_rava_michzei)
Rava: both clauses are mistaken purchases; in the first, not having paid, it does not look like an idol in a Jew's hand; in the latter, having paid, it does
ואביי אמר לך: the first, he did not know, not having paid; the latter -- having paid, he should have inspected and then pulled (= p_abaye_seifa_lav_mekach_taut)
Abaye: the latter clause is not a mistaken purchase -- having paid, when he pulled he should have inspected and then pulled
Ameimar: with a gentile, pulling acquires
Reish Lakish: pulling is explicit in the Torah
to your fellow you return overcharge (onaah); you do not return overcharge to a gentile
one [verse-word] for a gentile and one for hekdesh: there is no onaah for hekdesh either
one view: robbing a gentile is forbidden
[the tanna] holds: [retracting] words carries [the stigma of] lacking faith -- that is, Jew from Jew, for they stand by their word
